title: The Dumbest Mistake Leaders Make in Communication
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that the most common communication failure of middle managers is acting as a messenger who simply passes information up and down unchanged. He contends that a leader's job is to gather information, make sense of it, filter it, add context and own it before communicating. The piece then sets out what should flow upward (wins tied to business goals, a SWOT-style assessment with explicit asks, project status and operational metrics) and downward (leadership decisions with rationale, people changes, business updates, always inviting questions). Its organizing 'Magic Formula' is to be relevant and authentic, with checklists for testing relevance to each audience. Jain closes by distinguishing transparency from sharing everything verbatim, and by criticizing managers who 'pass the buck' on decisions they deliver.
points: Managers who merely relay information add no value; the leader's job is to process, filter, contextualize and own information before passing it on.
Upward communication should tie team wins to business goals and include concrete asks for resources and help, not a dump of everything happening.
Relevance is tested by audience: for leadership, what they can act on or need to weigh in on; for the team, what affects them and what they care about.
Authenticity means owning decisions when cascading them rather than saying 'It's HR's decision' or 'it's not my call'.
Transparency is honesty about what can and cannot be shared, not the verbatim sharing of everything.
quotes: Some managers like to share everything happening in their teams with their managers and leadership team. Others fall to the other extreme and share sparingly.
You are not the messenger. If you were, your job would have been automated and eliminated a long time ago, much before the AI bots descended on earth.

Celebrate your team’s recent accomplishments/wins. What’s really important here is to highlight how your team contributed to the business goals, and provided value to your customers. Remember that everything you and your team does should ultimately help the organization move towards the larger goals.

When communicating up, be genuine and honest with your information. For example, when sharing a team update, share it with authenticity, and represent your team like you are their voice. When asking for more resources, make an honest case backed by data and a genuine need.
When communicating down, be authentic and “own” the information you share. If there is negative news, share it with empathy, and with a human heart.
Again — you are not a messenger. Transparency does not mean that you share everything verbatim. It means you are honest and authentic.

As a leader, you need to own up to your team’s errors. You need to be accountable for their failures. You need to stand up in front of your teams, share negative news, and be open to facing difficult questions.
